title: A Brief History of Fashion Retail

paragraphs.text: During the European Renaissance (roughly 1300-1600), the process of purchasing clothing was vastly different from what it is today. Firstly, fabrics had to be bought from markets or travelling salesmen. Then, the fabrics would be taken to local dressmakers who would make up clothes and accessories. Buying garments could be a lengthy process, as the elements of an outfit were purchased from various shops and then made up by craftspeople.

During the 17th century, the English and Dutch East India Companies (EIC) improved trade links with Asia. By the mid-18th century, cotton from India was an everyday fabric throughout Europe. It was fashionable and, more significantly, it was cheap and washable, and therefore brought greater levels of cleanliness to people of all classes. Textiles and clothing such as silks and calicoes were relatively expensive, and given to cooks, cleaning maids and other domestic help, instead of their wages. They were then passed down through their families. What is more, when they were worn out, these old fabrics were sold to used clothing shops and markets and eventually they were turned into paper. In the 18th century, with better agricultural practices and distribution of wealth. more people wanted to buy fashionable clothes. Shopkeepers began to take more time over the display of their goods and their approach to customers.

By the 1780s, plate-glass windows led to attractive displays promoting a shop’s products, designed to encourage passersby to enter the shop and see the interior displays, which were becoming even more sophisticated.

In the early 1800s, the emergence of larger establishments that began to group together a wider range of goods and services signalled a new era in shopping. Aristide Boucicaut opened his Le Bon Marche in Paris in 1838, which by 1852 had evolved into a department store. It brought together fabrics and other fashionable products, and introduced a strong social element to shopping by providing a restaurant on one of its floors. Boucicaut developed various new sales techniques, which changed the relationships between shop workers and customers, and between customers and the way they used a shop. Unlike other stores, where customers could negotiate, his set prices were clearly shown on all goods. A further innovation was he also allowed people to have a refund if they changed their mind, or exchange the item for something else. His store, and others like it, developed increasingly sophisticated sales techniques. Shoppers were encouraged to browse. In order to achieve this, Boucicaut had mapped out strategically designed routes around the shop floors. In this way, customers could visit the different departments, or stop to watch the entertainment provided at no cost. For the first time, shopping became an activity for leisure, focused on spending time and money in a fashionable, secure environment.

In the 1700s, before the appearance of the department store, it had been impossible for middle-and upper-class women to go shopping alone. Even with an accompanying maid or footman, certain streets were out of bounds at particular times of the day. Bond Street in London, for example, was a focus for shops for gentlemen, and it was considered improper for ladies to go there during the afternoons. Later on, these careful rules of etiquette were eroded by department stores, which encouraged women to socialise and browse. This gave women greater freedom, and shaped them as consumers. Each store developed its own character, aiming to draw in customers who were attracted to their style, as well as to the diversity of their goods. Thus, in 1875, Liberty opened in London selling ornaments and fabrics like most other department stores. But what set it apart from others was the fact that it also stocked a wide range of furniture from Asia. Throughout the late 1800s, some stores opened branches in other towns or in the suburbs. Other stores launched branches in stylish seaside resorts. The spread of department stores brought fashionable goods to a wider range of people. Stores worked hard to build a relationship with their customers. winning their loyalty through services. quality and price.

The open design of department stores allowed a wide range of people to come in and look around. By the 1850s, the growth of public transport made shopping trips simple and affordable. Underground trains in major cities would make this process even easier, and encouraged the idea of a day’s shopping as a source of relaxation and fun.

In the 1800s, in cities throughout Europe and other western countries, stores worked hard to tempt shoppers with exciting new technology. For example, in 1898, Harrods in London attracted a large crowd and much press coverage for introducing escalators to take people from floor to floor.

In the early 20th century, mail-order shopping was another important innovation, particularly in countries such as America and Australia where the distances between cities made visiting shops in person difficult. Marshall Ward, a Chicago-based store, had a famous mail-order service whose eye-catching catalogues tempted Americans with their wide array of ready-to-wear clothing for the whole family.
